overview.intro:
Chapter 34 covers soap and liquid skin cleansers (3401), surfactants and washing and cleaning preparations such as laundry and dish detergents (3402), lubricating preparations (3403), artificial and prepared waxes (3404), polishes and scouring powders (3405), candles (3406), and modeling pastes and dental waxes (3407). Its 48 tariff lines carry base rates from **Free to 6.5%**, and the U.S. imported **$6.47B** of these goods in 2025; candles alone were $1.22B.

Unlike many chapters, Chapter 34 has **no general exemption** from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs: since July 24, 2026 goods of the 60 listed economies pay 10% or 12.5% on top of the base rate (a flat 10% for the EU, 12.5% for Japan and South Korea). USMCA goods of Canada and Mexico enter Free — except **candles of Canada, which pay 50%** under Section 338 since August 22, 2026, USMCA or not. Chinese goods pay the 12.5% plus their 2018–2019 Section 301 duties (25% on most lines), and petroleum wax candles from China are also under an **antidumping order** that the tariff calculator does not include. The IEEPA duties of 2025 ended on February 24, 2026.

productGroups.label: Soap & skin-washing preparations
productGroups.blurb: Bar soap (toilet, Castile, laundry bars), soap flakes and powders, liquid hand soap and body wash put up for retail sale, and wipes impregnated with soap or detergent: 6 lines, Free except 4% for liquid skin cleansers containing an aromatic surfactant (3401.30.10). Shampoos and bath preparations are not here (Chapter 33).

productGroups.label: Surfactants, detergents & cleaners
productGroups.blurb: Anionic, cationic and nonionic surfactants (LAS, sulfated alcohols), laundry and dishwashing detergents and cleaning preparations, retail or bulk: 22 lines at 3.7% to 6.5%, except Free for retail detergents with no aromatic surfactant (3402.50.51).

productGroups.label: Lubricating preparations
productGroups.blurb: Lubricants, greases, cutting oils, mold-release and anti-rust preparations, and textile or leather treatment preparations with less than 70% petroleum oil: 8 lines at 0.2% to 6.5%. Lubricants that are 70% or more petroleum oil are in Chapter 27.

productGroups.label: Artificial & prepared waxes
productGroups.blurb: Polyethylene glycol waxes, blended and chemically produced waxes, and prepared waxes containing bleached beeswax: 4 lines, all Free. Unmixed beeswax (1521) and paraffin wax (2712) are classified elsewhere.

productGroups.label: Polishes & scouring preparations
productGroups.blurb: Shoe polish, furniture and floor polish, car polishes, metal and glass polishes and scouring powders, including wipes impregnated with them: 5 lines, all Free.

productGroups.label: Candles
productGroups.blurb: Candles, tapers and the like, scented or not: one line, Free. Candles from China are also under a 1986 antidumping order, and Canadian candles pay a 50% Section 338 duty since August 22, 2026.

productGroups.label: Modeling pastes & dental waxes
productGroups.blurb: Modeling clay and play dough, dental waxes and impression compounds put up in sets or plates, and plaster-based dental preparations: 2 lines, both Free.

notes.chapterNotes:
**Note 1.** This chapter does not cover: (a) edible mixtures or preparations of animal, vegetable or microbial fats or oils of a kind used as mold release preparations (heading 1517); (b) separate chemically defined compounds; or (c) shampoos, dentifrices, shaving creams and foams or bath preparations, containing soap or other organic surface-active agents (heading 3305, 3306 or 3307).

**Note 2.** For the purposes of heading 3401, the expression "soap" applies only to soap soluble in water. Soap and the other products of heading 3401 may contain added substances (for example, disinfectants, abrasive powders, fillers or medicaments). Products containing abrasive powders remain classified in heading 3401 only if in the form of bars, cakes or molded pieces or shapes. In other forms they are to be classified in heading 3405 as "scouring powders and similar preparations".

**Note 3.** For the purposes of heading 3402, "organic surface-active agents" are products which when mixed with water at a concentration of 0.5 percent at 20°C and left to stand for one hour at the same temperature: (a) give a transparent or translucent liquid or stable emulsion without separation of insoluble matter; and (b) reduce the surface tension of water to 4.5 x 10⁻² N/m (45 dyne/cm) or less.

**Note 4.** In heading 3403 the expression "petroleum oils and oils obtained from bituminous minerals" applies to the products defined in note 2 to chapter 27.

**Note 5.** In heading 3404, subject to the exclusions provided below, the expression "artificial waxes and prepared waxes" applies only to: (a) chemically produced organic products of a waxy character, whether or not water-soluble; (b) products obtained by mixing different waxes; (c) products of a waxy character with a basis of one or more waxes and containing fats, resins, mineral substances or other materials. The heading does not apply to: (a) goods of heading 1516, 3402 or 3823 even if having a waxy character; (b) unmixed animal waxes or unmixed vegetable waxes, whether or not refined or colored, of heading 1521; (c) mineral waxes or similar products of heading 2712, whether or not intermixed or merely colored; or (d) waxes mixed with, dispersed in or dissolved in a liquid medium (headings 3405, 3809, etc.).

seo.shortDescription: What changed for soap, detergent, lubricant, wax and candle imports since January 2025: the IEEPA duties and their end, the Section 122 surcharge, the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies, 50% on Canadian candles and the China candle antidumping order, with Federal Register citations.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). All 48 Chapter 34 lines carry the same base rates in both — Free to 6.5%.

What changed were the extra duties. In 2025 Chapter 34 goods paid IEEPA duties: 25% (Canada later 35%) on non-USMCA goods of Canada and Mexico, fentanyl and reciprocal duties on China, and the reciprocal tariff on almost everyone else. Those duties **ended on February 24, 2026**, and the 10% **Section 122** surcharge that replaced them expired on July 23, 2026. Since **July 24, 2026** the **2026 Section 301 tariffs** on 60 economies apply to the whole chapter — there is no general exemption list for soap, detergents or candles — and USMCA goods of Canada and Mexico are exempt. Since **August 22, 2026** candles of Canada pay **50%** under Section 338, USMCA or not. China keeps its 2018–2019 Section 301 duties on top.

Separately, candles of petroleum wax from China have been under an **antidumping duty order** since 1986. It is listed below for reference; it is set exporter by exporter by the Commerce Department and is **not included in the tariff calculator**.

For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

changes.title: No Chapter 34 base-rate changes
changes.detail: All 48 Chapter 34 tariff lines carry the same General, Special and Column 2 rates in the 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition; no line was added, removed or renumbered.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on Nicaragua phases in from 2027
changes.detail: Products of Nicaragua that are not CAFTA-DR originating goods will pay +10% from January 1, 2027 and +15% from January 1, 2028 (9903.89.01, U.S. note 29), with no exemption for Chapter 34. The rate is 0% in 2026; Nicaragua's 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty (9903.05.58) applies meanwhile.

changes.title: China Section 301 duties continue during the four-year review
changes.detail: USTR received requests to continue the 2018 China actions, so they did not terminate on their July 6 and August 23, 2026 anniversaries and remain in effect pending the statutory review. Chapter 34 keeps List 3 (+25%), List 2 (+25%) and List 4A (+7.5%) duties.

changes.title: Sixth five-year review of the China candle antidumping order begins
changes.detail: Commerce and the ITC started the sixth sunset review of the 1986 antidumping duty order on petroleum wax candles from China (A-570-504; ITC 731-TA-282). Responses to the ITC were due October 1, 2026 and comments on their adequacy by November 16, 2026. The order stays in force during the review.

changes.title: 50% Section 338 duty on candles from Canada
changes.detail: Proclamation 11048 imposed additional duties under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 on a list of Canadian products to offset Canada's surtax on U.S. motor vehicles. Candles (3406.00.00) are on list (b)(3) of U.S. note 51 and pay +50% (9903.03.14) from August 22, 2026 (Proclamation 11056 moved the start from August 19), also when entered under USMCA. Proclamation 11065 changed the list from September 15, 2026 but kept candles. No other Chapter 34 line is covered.

changes.title: 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies reach all of Chapter 34
changes.detail: The 10% or 12.5% Section 301 duties on 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84) took effect. Chapter 34 has no general exemption under U.S. note 52(b): only five surfactant and soap subheadings are exempt when for pharmaceutical use (note 52(e)). USMCA goods of Canada and Mexico are exempt (9903.05.93, 9903.05.94). The EU pays a flat 10%, Japan and South Korea a flat 12.5%, where the base rate is lower.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day 10% surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026. It had applied to Chapter 34 goods of every country except the nonionic surfactants of 3402.42 (on the exemption list, 9903.03.03) and USMCA goods of Canada and Mexico (9903.03.07, 9903.03.08).

changes.title: Brazil Section 301 tariff reaches all of Chapter 34
changes.detail: The 25% Section 301 duty on goods of Brazil (9903.05.01) took effect. No Chapter 34 line is on the Brazil exemption list (U.S. note 50(a)(ii)); the five pharmaceutical-use subheadings are exempt only for that use (note 50(a)(v), 9903.05.06). From July 24 the 12.5% 60-economy duty is added.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S) still remove the base rate and the 10% Section 301 duty on Canada and Mexico.

changes.title: Section 232 aluminum duty no longer reaches Chapter 34 (except Russia)
changes.detail: Proclamation 11021 rebuilt the metals tariffs around new product lists (U.S. note 16(c)) and ended the duties on derivative articles left off them. No Chapter 34 line is on the new lists, so the aluminum-content duty that 16 Chapter 34 subheadings paid from August 18, 2025 stopped. Russia's 200% duty on derivative aluminum articles (9903.85.68, note 19(k)) still covers them.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs
changes.detail: A 10% surcharge on products of all countries (9903.03.01) applied until July 23, 2026. Only the 3402.42 nonionic surfactants were on its product exemption list (9903.03.03); USMCA goods of Canada and Mexico were exempt.

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24. For Chapter 34 this removed the 35% (Canada) and 25% (Mexico) duties on non-USMCA goods, the 10% fentanyl and 10% reciprocal duties on China, and the reciprocal rates on other countries.

changes.title: China exclusion for subheading 3401.19 soap extended to November 9, 2026
changes.detail: USTR extended 178 Section 301 product exclusions, including the one for 3401.19.00.00 (other soap and organic surface-active products in bars, cakes or molded shapes, and impregnated paper and nonwovens), which removes the 7.5% List 4A duty (9903.88.69). The exclusion runs through November 9, 2026.

changes.title: China fentanyl duty cut from 20% to 10%

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 34 goods were **$6.47B in 2025**, -0.2% on 2024 and up from $5.10B in 2020. **Canada** ($1.18B) and **Mexico** ($1.04B) supply 34%, mostly detergents and cleaning preparations ($674M from Mexico and $419M from Canada in heading 3402) and soap, which enter Free when they qualify for USMCA. Germany ($516M) leads in lubricating preparations and waxes.

**Candles** are the largest single line at $1.22B (19% of the chapter). **Vietnam** shipped $659M of them — 54% — and Canada $256M, while China, whose petroleum wax candles have been under an antidumping order since 1986, shipped only $43M. China is still a major supplier of soap ($331M) and modeling clay ($161M), but its total fell to $666M from $798M in 2024 and $1.06B in 2020.

The 2026 changes are not in these figures yet: the Section 301 duty on 60 economies (from July 24, 2026) and the 50% Section 338 duty on Canadian candles (from August 22, 2026) apply to the largest non-USMCA suppliers and to Canada's $256M of candles. 2025 is the latest full year of U.S. trade data. Duty-collected figures aren't available from an official source yet.

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 34: Soap, Detergents, Waxes & Candles — Import Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Soap, Detergent & Candles: FDA, EPA, CPSC Rules & Legal Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 34) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The rules for each HTS Chapter 34 line — FDA's soap vs cosmetic vs drug line, antibacterial soap ingredients, EPA registration for disinfecting cleaners, TSCA certification, the CPSC lead-wick candle ban, aerosol hazmat — the China candle antidumping order, and legal ways to pay less duty.

tariffEngineering.intro:
What decides the duty on Chapter 34 goods today is mostly **origin**: USMCA goods of Canada and Mexico enter Free (except Canadian candles, 50%), the 60 Section 301 economies pay 10% or 12.5% on top of a base rate of up to 6.5%, and Chinese goods pay up to 37.5% more. Candles of petroleum wax from China also carry an **antidumping duty** that the tariff calculator does not include.

The paperwork depends on what the product claims to do. FDA decides whether a cleanser is "soap", a cosmetic or an over-the-counter drug; EPA registers cleaners that claim to disinfect; most chemical products need a TSCA certification; CPSC bans lead-cored candle wicks; and aerosol lubricants and polishes are hazardous materials in transport. Each rule and lever below links to its regulation.

levers.title: Claim USMCA for Canadian and Mexican goods
levers.saves: The base rate (up to 6.5%) and the 10% Section 301 duty on Canada (9903.05.29) or Mexico (9903.05.55): a 3.7% detergent goes from 13.7% to Free
levers.appliesTo: All 48 lines, for originating goods of Canada or Mexico (not the 50% on Canadian candles)
levers.document: A USMCA certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer, meeting the Chapter 34 product-specific rule in General Note 11: a change of heading for soap (3401) and for polishes, candles and modeling pastes (3405–3407); a change of subheading, or a regional value content of at least 60% (transaction value) or 50% (net cost), for surfactants, lubricants and waxes (3402–3404).
levers.caveat: The 50% Section 338 duty on Canadian candles applies even under USMCA. The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

citations.label: HTSUS General Note 11 (USMCA rules of origin)
HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 51 and 52(g)–(h)

levers.title: Compare supplier countries — the extra duty ranges from 0 to 37.5%
levers.saves: Up to 37.5% of value: for candles, 12.5% from Vietnam, 10% from India or the EU, Free from Mexico under USMCA, against 20% plus antidumping duty from China and 50% from Canada
levers.document: Commercial invoice and production records showing where the goods were made. For blends and refills, origin follows where the goods were last substantially transformed; ask CBP for a binding ruling when a Chinese concentrate is diluted or packed elsewhere.
levers.caveat: Diluting, mixing or repacking in a third country does not always change origin. The antidumping order follows its own scope and country rules, separate from the tariff origin.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 20 and 52

levers.title: Claim the pharmaceutical-use exemption for listed surfactants
levers.saves: The 10% or 12.5% Section 301 duty (and Brazil's 25%) on goods for use in pharmaceutical applications
levers.document: Entry under 9903.05.89 (Brazil: 9903.05.06) with records showing the goods are for use in pharmaceutical applications.
levers.caveat: Only those five subheadings and only that end use; the same surfactants for detergents or cosmetics pay the duty. It does not remove China's List 3 duty.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 50(a)(v) and 52(e)

levers.title: Get the line right — several pairs differ only by formula
levers.saves: Up to 6.5% of value: liquid skin cleansers and retail detergents are Free unless they contain an aromatic or modified aromatic surfactant (then 4%); lubricants with 50% or more petroleum oil pay 0.2% instead of 1.4% to 6.1%
levers.document: The formula (surfactant types, petroleum-oil content) and, when the line is unclear, a binding ruling from CBP before importing.
levers.caveat: Classification follows the goods as imported; change the formula only for real product reasons. Shampoo, bath foam and shaving cream are Chapter 33, and lubricants with 70% or more petroleum oil Chapter 27 (chapter note 1; heading 3403).

levers.title: Check the candle antidumping scope before buying from China
levers.saves: The whole antidumping duty, when the candle is outside the order
levers.document: The order's written scope: candles made from petroleum wax with fiber or paper-cored wicks, in the listed shapes. When a candle's wax blend or shape makes coverage unclear, request a scope ruling from Commerce.
levers.caveat: A candle inside the scope pays the cash deposit at the exporter's rate whatever its HTS line. Antidumping duties cannot be refunded as drawback.

levers.title: Claim drawback on goods that are exported
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the duties paid on goods re-exported unused or used to make exported products
levers.document: A drawback claim to CBP with import and export records (19 CFR part 191). CBP's Section 301 FAQ says Section 301 duties are eligible for drawback.
levers.caveat: Antidumping and countervailing duties are not refundable as drawback (19 CFR 191.3(b)(3)).

rules.title: Soap vs cosmetic: only alkali salts of fatty acids sold only as soap are "soap" (outside FDA's cosmetic rules); synthetic-detergent cleansers for the body are cosmetics
Cosmetics (liquid hand soap, body wash): facility registration and product listing under the Modernization of Cosmetics Regulation Act of 2022

citations.label: FDA: Registration and Listing of Cosmetic Product Facilities and Products

rules.title: Antibacterial (antiseptic) hand and body washes are OTC drugs: washes with any of 19 listed ingredients, including triclosan and triclocarban, need FDA new-drug approval, and foreign drug establishments must register with FDA
Cleaners and wipes that claim to disinfect or kill germs are pesticides: EPA registration and a Notice of Arrival before the shipment arrives
Chemical substances and mixtures (surfactants, detergents, lubricants, waxes): TSCA import certification (positive or negative) at entry
Candles with metal-cored wicks: banned unless the core is no more than 0.06% lead, and shipping cartons must say "Conforms to 16 CFR 1500.17(a)(13)"
Modeling clay and dough for children: art-material hazard labeling (ASTM D-4236) and a Children's Product Certificate
Products in aerosol cans (spray lubricants, polishes, foaming cleansers): hazardous materials (UN1950) for shipping papers, marking and packaging
Petroleum wax candles from China: antidumping duty cash deposit at the exporter's rate (not in the tariff calculator)
Country-of-origin marking on each retail article or its container (soap bars, detergent bottles, candles)

groups.label: Soap & skin-washing preparations
groups.note: Which agency applies depends on the claims: true soap sold only as soap is outside FDA's cosmetic rules; other body cleansers are cosmetics; antibacterial washes are OTC drugs; wipes claiming to disinfect need EPA registration.

groups.label: Surfactants, detergents & cleaners
groups.note: Bulk surfactants and detergents need a TSCA certification. Cleaners that claim to disinfect or sanitize are pesticides under EPA rules. The nonionic surfactants of 3402.42 were the only Chapter 34 lines exempt from the 2025 reciprocal tariff and the Section 122 surcharge.

groups.label: Lubricating preparations
groups.note: Lubricants with 70% or more petroleum oil are classified in Chapter 27. Spray lubricants in aerosol cans are hazardous materials in transport.

groups.label: Artificial & prepared waxes
groups.note: Unmixed beeswax (1521) and paraffin wax (2712) are not in this heading. No antidumping order covers waxes.

groups.label: Polishes & scouring preparations
groups.note: Aerosol polishes are hazardous materials in transport. Polishes in liquid or paste form, including waxes dispersed in a liquid, belong here rather than in 3404 (chapter note 5).

groups.label: Candles
groups.note: Candles of petroleum wax from China are under the 1986 antidumping order (sixth review started September 1, 2026); candles of Canada pay 50% under Section 338 since August 22, 2026.

groups.label: Modeling pastes & dental waxes
groups.note: Modeling pastes are not on any China Section 301 list, so Chinese modeling clay pays only the 12.5% 2026 duty.

tariffEngineering.disclaimer: A checklist of where the rules are, with links to the regulations — not legal advice. Antidumping rates are exporter-specific and change with each administrative review; check Commerce's latest notice and CBP's cash-deposit instructions before importing candles from China.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for soap?
faqs.answer: Heading 3401. Toilet soap in bars is 3401.11 (Castile soap 3401.11.10, other 3401.11.50); other bar soap, such as laundry bars, 3401.19; soap flakes, powder and paste 3401.20; liquid or cream skin cleansers put up for retail sale 3401.30. All are Free except 3401.30.10, 4%, for skin cleansers containing an aromatic surfactant. Shampoo, shaving cream and bath preparations are Chapter 33 (chapter note 1), and soap dishes and dispensers are not in Chapter 34.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for liquid hand soap and body wash?
searchedAs: hs code for liquid body wash
hs code for hand wash liquid
faqs.answer: 3401.30: organic surface-active products for washing the skin, in liquid or cream form, put up for retail sale. 3401.30.50 is Free; 3401.30.10, for products containing an aromatic or modified aromatic surfactant, is 4%. From China they pay 37.5% more (Section 301 List 3 plus the 2026 12.5%); from the EU a flat 10%; from Mexico or Canada under USMCA nothing.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for candles?
faqs.answer: 3406.00.00 — candles, tapers and the like, scented or not and whatever the wax. It is a single U.S. line with a Free general rate. Candle holders and candlesticks are not in Chapter 34.

faqs.question: What are the U.S. tariffs on candles?
faqs.answer: The base rate is Free, so the duty is the extra tariff for the country: 12.5% from Vietnam (the largest supplier, $659M in 2025), 10% from India or the UK, a flat 10% from the EU, Free from Mexico under USMCA, 50% from Canada (Section 338, even under USMCA), and 20% from China plus an antidumping duty on petroleum wax candles.

faqs.question: Is there an antidumping duty on candles from China?
searchedAs: anti dumping duty on candles from china
faqs.answer: Yes. Petroleum wax candles from China have been under an antidumping duty order since 1986. Commerce continued it on October 29, 2021, finding that revocation would likely lead to dumping margins of up to 104.33%, and a sixth five-year review began on September 1, 2026. The cash deposit depends on the exporter and is paid on top of the tariff: 7.5% Section 301 List 4A plus the 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty. U.S. imports of candles from China were only $43M in 2025.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for laundry detergent and dish soap?
searchedAs: hs code for laundry detergent pods
faqs.answer: Washing and cleaning preparations put up for retail sale — laundry detergent (powder, liquid or pods) and dishwashing liquid — are 3402.50: 3402.50.11 (4%) if they contain an aromatic or modified aromatic surfactant, otherwise 3402.50.51 (Free). The same preparations not for retail sale are 3402.90 (3.7% to 4%). Laundry soap in bars is 3401.19 and soap powder 3401.20.

faqs.question: What does HS code 3402 cover?
faqs.answer: Organic surface-active agents other than soap and the preparations made from them: linear alkylbenzene sulfonic acids and salts (3402.31), other anionic surfactants (3402.39), cationic (3402.41), nonionic (3402.42) and other surfactants (3402.49), retail washing and cleaning preparations (3402.50) and other preparations (3402.90). Rates are 3.7% to 6.5%, except Free for 3402.50.51. It is the largest Chapter 34 heading by value: $2.18B of imports in 2025.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for lubricants and grease?
faqs.answer: Heading 3403 covers lubricating preparations, cutting oils, mold-release and anti-rust preparations with less than 70% by weight of petroleum oil; with 70% or more they are petroleum oils of Chapter 27 (2710). Within 3403, preparations with 50% or more petroleum oil pay 0.2% (3403.11.20, 3403.19.10); others 1.4% to 6.5% (3403.99.00, other lubricating preparations, 6.5%). Spray lubricants in aerosol cans are hazardous materials in transport.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for wax and candle wax?
faqs.answer: Artificial and prepared waxes — blends of different waxes, chemically produced waxes and polyethylene glycol waxes — are heading 3404 (3404.20, 3404.90), all Free. Under chapter note 5, unmixed beeswax and other unmixed animal or vegetable waxes are heading 1521, and paraffin and other mineral waxes heading 2712. Finished candles are 3406.00.00.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for shoe polish and car wax?
searchedAs: hs code for car wax polish
faqs.answer: Heading 3405, all Free: polishes and creams for footwear or leather 3405.10, for wooden furniture and floors 3405.20, for car bodywork 3405.30, scouring pastes and powders 3405.40, and other polishes such as metal or glass polish 3405.90. Waxes dispersed in a liquid medium belong here rather than in 3404 (chapter note 5). From China they pay 37.5% more.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for modeling clay and play dough?
faqs.answer: 3407.00.20 — modeling pastes, including those put up for children's amusement; dental waxes and impression compounds are 3407.00.40. Both are Free, and neither is on a China Section 301 list, so Chinese modeling clay pays only the 12.5% 2026 duty. China shipped $161M of heading 3407 in 2025. Children's modeling compounds need art-material labeling and a Children's Product Certificate.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on soap imported from China?
faqs.answer: Most Chinese soap pays its base rate plus 37.5%: 25% under Section 301 List 3 (9903.88.03) and 12.5% under the 2026 action (9903.05.31). Subheading 3401.19.00 (other soap in bars and soap- or detergent-impregnated paper and nonwovens) is on List 4A instead, and a USTR exclusion removes that 7.5% through November 9, 2026, so it pays 12.5%. The IEEPA duties on China ended February 24, 2026.

faqs.question: What does HTS Chapter 34 cover?
faqs.answer: Soap, organic surface-active agents, washing preparations, lubricating preparations, artificial and prepared waxes, polishing and scouring preparations, candles, modeling pastes, dental waxes and plaster-based dental preparations: headings 3401 to 3407, split into 48 ten-digit U.S. lines with base rates from Free to 6.5%. U.S. imports were $6.47B in 2025.
